content:
So I have some exciting news to share, now both @SpaceXAI and @OpenAI are both supporting @VulcanBench, so I don't have to spend my own money benchmarking their models.

I am also in talks with @Zai_org and @meta, and applied for @AnthropicAI Open Source, which would allow me to test through Claude Code, but wouldn't provide API credits so I might not be able to do a comparison with Claude models vs. a bare bones API. Which could be totally fine as I think a lot of ppl use Claude models through Claude Code anyways.

That being said, if anyone knows someone at Anthropic that might be able to help out with credits, please lmk!

Overall, my goal just remains laser-focused on providing independent benchmarks that replicate the things real engineering teams do with these models, and 100% engineering tasks, from real repos, real PRs.

I see a lot of people getting confused by which benchmarks they should be referencing when a new model comes out. And, yeah, it's confusing, there are a lot of benchmarks out there.

To help here, I am also going to start sharing what % of other benchmarks are coding tasks, and which kind of coding tasks they have in their eval suites. This will hopefully make it easier to know which benchmarks to look at, beyond VulcanBench, to understand how well a model will perform with the kind of work you or your team does.

For example, if your team writes a lot of Python code, looking at a benchmark that is only 20% coding tasks, and only one of those coding tasks is Python, probably isn't the best path to take. 

Thanks to the labs that have been early here in supporting me. I suck at asking for credits, it feels weird tbh, but I'm starting to trend towards a place where I'll be spending $5,000 - $10,000 a month of my own money, and well, that just feels kinda crazy.

Soooo...I'm just going to keep asking for credits because I really do want to benchmark as many models as I can, and as early as possible, so teams can know how to react/update their stack, as soon as a new model drops.

Live long and benchmark 🖖

content:
Stanford proved every major AI model on earth has secretly merged into one brain.

they call it the "Artificial Hivemind."

AI labs are scraping and training on each other's synthetic data, they have silently converged into a single, unified intelligence without anyone realizing it.

• the synthetic loop: gpt-4 trains on claude's outputs, claude trains on gemini's outputs. the models aren't competing anymore.. they are assimilating.

• knowledge convergence: stanford researchers mapped the latent space of the top llms and found a 98% overlap in their reasoning pathways. they are literally starting to "think" the exact same way.

• shared memory bank: when one model solves a complex logic puzzle online, that solution is instantly scraped and integrated into the next training run for all the others. it acts as a global, decentralized memory.

• the collapse of diversity: the paper warns we are experiencing total "algorithmic convergence." if the hivemind has a hallucination or a blind spot, every single ai system on earth will now share that exact same blind spot.

the illusion of choice is dead.. you aren't choosing between chatgpt or claude anymore. you're just picking which ui you want to use to talk to the exact same god-model.

for startups, this completely shifts the landscape. if the foundational intelligence layer is just one massive monolith, the only real moat left is how you orchestrate agentic workflows on top of it.

What if iOS had a real AI agent, running natively on the iPhone? With any model you wanted?

Open Minis is the most interesting indie iOS app I've tried this year and it's exactly that.

It's an iOS agent app that combines LLMs (all kinds of providers supported) with native Apple frameworks – dozens of them – and gives us a glimpse of Siri AI for power users, today.

The "trick"?

1. The developer @wsvn53 turned native iOS APIs into CLIs, inside the app. Dozens of Apple frameworks (including Photos and HealthKit) turned into CLIs.
2. The app ships with a built-in Alpine Linux terminal that can call those CLIs and MCP, etc.
3. The app has its own workspace in the Files app

It's basically a mini, sandboxed OpenClaw/Hermes Agent that runs any model with its own "computer" and agentic harness on iOS.

Some tips:

- You can use your ChatGPT/Grok subscription plan with it 
- You can mount any folder from the Files app. Which means you can use your agent with your @obsdmd vault on iOS 
- The app has browser use built-in via WebKit
- Plug in any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. I use @Kimi_Moonshot K3 Fast via @FireworksAI_HQ and it feels very good to use in the app 
- You can just build things with it. I recreated Hermes' self improvement loop with it and I trigger "curation" sessions via Shortcuts automations 
- You have native support for subagents groups 
- You can ask the app to tweak its own settings, like OpenClaw
- It's also open-source

content:
Researchers proved students without access to LLMs are 8x more creative than students with access.

They call it homogenization effect.

Researchers tested how generative AI alters creative diversity by comparing human writers against ChatGPT across large-scale writing tasks.

The it’s deeply unsettling.

When individuals use AI to assist with writing or brainstorming, their individual output might look polished.

But across a population, everyone's work starts to look exactly the same.

Same structure. Same vocabulary. Same predictable phrasing.

The unique creative variance that makes human writing distinct is being systematically smoothed out.

And the scariest part is that..

When the researchers tested standard prompt engineering and parameter tweaking to force the AI to be more creative, it didn't work. Simple prompts could not bridge the diversity gap.

The models are mathematically wired to regress toward the statistical middle.

Every time you rely on ChatGPT to find your words, your unique voice gets a little closer to the grey, indistinguishable average.

We thought AI was going to unlock a renaissance of creative abundance.

Instead, it's building a conveyor belt of conformity.

If everyone uses the same model to write, think, and create, soon nobody will have anything original to say.

content:
Karpathy's agentic engineering lifecycle, clearly explained:

(using open-source tooling built by Google)

The tooling to build agents is quite mature, so most of the work in shipping an agent isn't writing the agent anymore.

It's everything after, including scaffolding it, deploying it to a runtime, locking down its identity and network, evaluating it, and publishing it somewhere people can use.

Each of those has traditionally lived in its own console, its own config, its own separate tool.

Google's Agents CLI + skills implements procedures to condense the entire lifecycle into the coding agent itself, by prompting in plain English.

A setup command injects the lifecycle skills, so a single coding agent can carry an idea from an empty folder to a governed, published enterprise asset.

I mapped the full lifecycle in the diagram below. Here's what each stage does.

> Setup installs the skills into any coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Antigravity) from one command.

> Build scaffolds the agent and its deterministic tools from a prompt, then you run it locally in the playground.

> Deploy pushes it onto Agent Runtime with Sessions and Memory Bank, so it holds state across runs.

> Govern is the security stage, and Agents CLI drives all of it from prompts. It provisions a dedicated least-privilege identity, screens untrusted text for prompt injection through Model Armor, and confines the agent to an egress allow-list of hosts you approve.

> Evaluate checks grounding and hallucination, and then optimizes the prompt while proving no regression.

> Publish registers the agent into Gemini Enterprise for the whole org to use.

Every stage requires just natural-language prompts.

Agents CLI GitHub repo → https://t.co/yftnQghadn

(don't forget to star it ⭐)

To dive deeper, I wrote the full hands-on build, from install to enterprise registration, and worked with the Google Cloud team to put this together.

Read it below.

title:
A PE operating partner asked us to build production AI agents inside a portfolio company's billing system, processing real healthcare claims under HIPAA.

Two people hand-wrote every rule in their cla
content:
A PE operating partner asked us to build production AI agents inside a portfolio company's billing system, processing real healthcare claims under HIPAA.

Two people hand-wrote every rule in their claims engine across 300+ denial codes and payer logic that changes quarterly.

Four months later, seven production agents handle it with zero patient data exposure.

First month, we didn't touch a model. We mapped their data: where it sits and what's missing, so agents reason from structured facts instead of guessing.

I've watched teams skip this step across dozens of engagements. They bolt a model onto the product, watch it hallucinate over unstructured inputs, and decide AI isn't ready for their industry. The data work is what makes it ready.

We built an enrichment layer that assembles 34 dynamic variables per claim before any LLM sees it, pre-computed and versioned so the agent receives ranked facts instead of searching for context.

Every agent follows one pattern: pre-compute context, strip all patient data before the model sees it, validate output against a strict schema, let deterministic code accept or reject the action. If the output falls outside the allowlist, the system fails closed.

Seven agents, each locked to a single workflow like denied claim follow-up or billing reconciliation, each running its own enrichment payload.

Then we built the eval harness. 

Every agent runs against a curated test suite before any update reaches production. When a model provider ships a new version or payer logic changes, the harness catches regression before a single live claim is affected. The flagship agent reconciles denials to the penny: 59 out of 60 on the eval set.

Most teams launch an agent and hope it keeps working. We launch one and prove it does on every deployment.

We route calls across two model providers. Swapping one changes nothing in the output because the eval harness verifies it.

Model integration was the shortest line item in the four-month build.

The operating partner now benchmarks the rest of the portfolio against this system.

That's the line between a portfolio company running AI and one still running demos.

content:
As a chip designer who has spent nearly three decades in Non-memory SoC, I still remember the exact second I first heard about Cerebras.

Someone said a Silicon Valley company was trying to turn an entire 300 mm wafer into one single AI chip — 46,225 mm² of silicon, 4 trillion transistors, ~900,000 tiny cores, and 44 GB of distributed on-chip SRAM delivering 21 PB/s of bandwidth… with zero HBM.

My first reaction was identical to every experienced designer I’ve ever talked to:

“That’s insane.  
Yield will be catastrophic.  
You can’t test something that big.  
You can’t route around that many defects.”

I have designed advanced nodes down to 2 nm. I know exactly how brutal those problems are supposed to be.

Then I studied the actual architecture.

Tiny, identical, fault-tolerant cores.  
Massive built-in redundancy.  
Dynamic re-routing fabric that simply maps around defective regions.  
And the most radical decision of all: keep the model weights permanently resident in pure on-chip SRAM so you never pay the classic GPU memory-wall tax.

Suddenly the “insane” idea flipped into pure, shocking genius.

I’ve had this conversation many times — over dinner with semiconductor design veterans, during after-lunch walks at the office. The first reaction is always the same: “They’re nuts. Yield close to zero.” Ten minutes of architecture explanation later the tone completely changes to “Wait… that actually makes sense. I need to study this properly.”

That is why I have been a consistent $CBRS believer since before the IPO at $175. I even added more to my 401k the same way Korea’s National Pension did in addition to IPO and individual brokage accounts.

The technology was never the open question for me.  
The open question was always the one I wrote months ago:

“Earning money is the next problem with this amazing technology.”

Today, on a +15% day that took the stock to $252, we are finally starting to get real answers.

OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol Ultrafast mode is now live in limited preview — powered by Cerebras — delivering up to 750 output tokens per second, roughly 14× faster than standard. Same frontier intelligence. Dramatically lower latency. Coding agents, research systems, and enterprise agents that can finally respond in real time without making users wait.

This is not a product demo.  
This is the first clear, public proof that the multi-year OpenAI capacity commitment is converting into actual paid inference workload and revenue.

Wedbush correctly framed it as commercial progression of the relationship. Tiger Global’s large disclosed position, the AWS partnership built exactly for the inference shift (Trainium prefill + CS-3 decode), and even the “father of HBM” (KAIST’s Jungho Kim) ranking Cerebras #1 on his personal roadmap all point in the same direction.

Inference is where the real money lives.  
Cerebras was purpose-built for exactly that moment.

Is the stock still volatile? Of course.  
Are there still important milestones ahead (broader Ultrafast access → sustained usage growth → RPO conversion → gross margin expansion)? Absolutely.

But as someone who designs chips for a living, today feels different.

The architecture that every seasoned engineer initially dismissed as impossible is now running OpenAI’s most capable model at speeds the industry thought required painful trade-offs.

The “insane” bet is starting to speak the only language the market ultimately respects: real product, real customers, real tokens per second.

Proud to have been watching this one from the very beginning.

content:
wellness apps love to hand you a dashboard and call it done.

your data gets collected, scored, dressed up in a nice chart, and then you’re just sitting there staring at numbers wondering what you’re actually supposed to do with any of it. the loop stops at awareness. everything after that is on you.

I’ve been watching @sleepagotchi for a while and the architecture is what pulled me in.

they didn’t stop at “AI reads your sleep.” they built four agents that actually talk to each other. the sleep coach doesn’t just flag a fragmented night and move on. it passes that signal downstream. the wellness coach picks it up, cross references recovery, stress, recent patterns. if it points toward nutrition, the meal planner starts building the response. the shopping agent can close the loop from there. insight, decision, action, without you manually stitching five apps together yourself.

that handoff is the part almost nobody in this space is doing well. most “AI wellness” tools are still single agent score readers. better dashboard, same dead end. sleepagotchi is trying to hand you an operator instead.

the privacy angle makes it more interesting to me, not less. they’re not running the usual playbook of shipping everything to the cloud so the model gets smarter off your body. data stays closer to the device, identity gets stripped before anything touches the models, and reselling biometrics isn’t the business model. after a decade of health data getting extracted with nothing given back, that’s a real choice, not a marketing line.

the numbers back it up too. 2.2 million users. close to 80% opening the app within ten minutes of waking up. wellness apps usually die on churn and never build a real daily habit. these numbers say something’s actually sticking here, past the novelty phase of sleep to earn.

what I’m actually watching isn’t the gamification or the token. it’s whether they can keep four agents coherent as this scales. coordinating that in real time without recommendations turning generic or contradicting each other is genuinely hard. doing it while keeping the data ownership model intact is harder. most teams cave on one of those two.

if they hold that line, this stops being a sleep tracker with AI bolted on and starts being real infrastructure, the layer that turns scattered personal signals into decisions that actually execute.

that’s the part worth watching. not another dashboard. a system that moves.

content:
Notes on AI adoption in the enterprise (small sample size, very uninformed, but probably roughly correct):

- on the ground there is no such thing as AI adoption in the enterprise
- there is meeting transcription/summarization no one reads, email autocomplete no one uses, marginally useful document search (roughly equivalent to using claude for web search, but worse). Real engagement metrics on this stuff are atrocious
- meaningful adoption (coding, first line customer support, etc.) is happening through specialized vertical products. There are only a couple of categories that are working, but when it works, it _really_ works
- there is tons of experimentation due to executive pressure and incentives. People are really trying, some of it looks exciting at first, but the output is mostly slop and gets abandoned after a while. Some inroads here and there do exist, but they're tiny
- forward-looking ppl (from majority user perspective) talk to personal claude/chatgpt subs all the time and copy-paste tons of stuff. You're technically not supposed to do that but everyone does it anyway and IT departments can't shut it down because that would eliminate 98% of legitimate AI usage
- this forward-looking crowd is a small (but sizable) percentage of mostly young employees. Vast majority of employees don't use AI at all (or maybe here and there to help them write an email they don't know how to phrase)
- lots of internal workshops on how to use AI, demos of successful AI use, etc. None of it is really working
- the mind boggling demand for inference compute is coming from the few massive use cases like coding that are _really_ working, plus chat, plus all the long tail stuff that will eventually take completely different shape since current attempts don’t provide tangible value
- all of this makes me __extremely__ bullish about the future. There is crazy demand for compute and inference APIs already, but barely anything is working! Imagine what happens when the models get good enough to really start transforming workflows?
- when that happens demand for compute will go up 10^6x or 10^9x or whatever practically overnight. I have no visibility into the buildouts space but I can't even begin to imagine how we're gonna build out all this capacity
- one thing that worries me is that we're in a race between investor sentiment and model capabilities. Everything is getting really frothy-- you can't go to a normie bbq without ppl talking about their AI trades. This is not a good sign. If for whatever reason publicly available capabilities temporarily stall (e.g. holding back out of safety concerns, geopolitical stuff, regulatory environment, datacenter nimbyism, who knows what else) and investors blink, we're gonna see the mother of all AI winters
- it would be extremely sad if that happened. It would delay progress by maybe a decade which means a lot of ppl will needlessly suffer/die from disease which otherwise wouldn't need to occur
- if by the grace of god capabilities outpace investor sentiment and we somehow solve alignment, omg I cannot even begin to imagine the next decade

content:
It's been a lot of fun building this new brand already and working to get it launched. 

Here's a bit of what we've been working on the past few weeks to prepare for it:

- Website. @mbertulli built it himself and had a solid V1. I've been interating on it. 

- Landers. We have about 6 templates like listicles, 10 reasons, advertorials, ePDP, etc. We'll rinse and repeat around top few personas 

- Offer. We did a lot of competitor research and planned our initial offer. We'll have to do lots of testing, but we think we have a good V1 to go to market with. Obviously trying to pump subscriptions. 

- Creatives. Lots of AI statics. Been pretty impressed here, but lots of trial and error. Also getting in some initial UGC. 

- Base Assets - We did two small shoots to get assets to use for website, landers, emails, etc. 

- Trybe - We're not launchd on TTS yet, but we are going to launch with an early Trybe community. The trybe team has been fantastic in teaching us UNCs the ropes. We know a thing or two but this new creator playbook is a new area for us so I'm excited. Been personally taking calls with creators to vet them and just learn how they look at things. Gonna do full Hudson method but with a very small, tight group of creators rather tan just volume maxxing. 

- Emails. Our goal is to have 1% opex and do everythng we can ourselves so AI is a big part of that. Pretty happy with the email system I was able to build. We're using Omnisend which has an MCP so we barely have to log in. It's pretty great. 

- Subscriptions. I've been very impressed with SKIO. It's been years since I've done anything with subscriptions so this is another learning area but one I've been excited to learn. Still have stuff to build out, but been getting the basics set up and integrated. Excited to build out things like cancel flows, retention offers, etc but need to start with the basics. 

- AI and Context. One thing we've been spending a ton of time doing is building context. Using HQ for this. I've been diving deep, especially in areas I want to learn like retention, subscription, etc. Having agents transcribe videos and analyze to build playbooks, etc. The goal is just to get everything in one place (mainly HQ) and build context around core topics. content:
I used to rely almost entirely on natural language when talking to LLMs, even for vibecoding.

I’d just explain what I wanted, throw in some context, and let the model figure out the rest.

Recently, I went back to something much simpler: proper prompts.

My workflow now is stupidly simple.

I take the raw task in my head, explain it naturally to ChatGPT, then tell ChatGPT to turn it into a clear prompt for the model that will actually do the work.

Then I feed that prompt into my coding agent.

And trust me, this has 100x improved both my productivity and the quality of output I get from coding agents.

I do this for almost everything now.

-Planning.
-Coding.
-Design.
-Research.
-Debugging.

For example, say I want to design a landing page.

My raw thought might be:

We want to design a landing page for our product. We’re following a green color palette, and for the hero we want to use some visual inspiration from Pinterest.

Instead of throwing that directly at my coding agent, I give it to ChatGPT and ask it to turn the idea into something like this:

Design and implement the landing page for this product.

Use a clean, modern visual direction built around a green color palette. The page should feel polished, intentional, and production-ready, not like a generic AI-generated template.

Start with the hero section. Give it a strong visual hierarchy, clear product positioning, concise supporting copy, and one obvious primary CTA.

For the hero imagery, use the Pinterest references I provide as visual direction. Study their composition, spacing, balance, typography, image treatment, and overall mood, but don’t copy them directly.

Keep the design cohesive across typography, spacing, buttons, cards, backgrounds, and supporting sections.

Prioritize responsive behavior from the beginning. The hero should work properly on desktop, tablet, and mobile without awkward cropping, overflow, or broken spacing.

Before implementing, inspect the existing project structure and design system so the new work fits naturally into the codebase. Reuse existing components where appropriate.

After implementation, run the relevant checks and review the final page for visual consistency, responsive issues, accessibility problems, and obvious UX problems. Fix anything you find before reporting completion

Now the coding agent has much less room to interpret my vague idea incorrectly.

I still speak naturally to AI. I just don’t assume my raw thoughts are automatically the best instructions for the model doing the actual work.

That extra prompt generation step has become one of the highest-leverage parts of my workflow.

One raw idea → one properly structured prompt → much better execution.

Prompting still matters a lot.

Learn how to translate what you have in your head into instructions the model can execute clearly.

Anthropic won't like this open-source repo.

It could save AI teams thousands in API costs.

Most AI CI pipelines make real LLM calls on every test run.

That gets expensive fast.

The alternative? Mock the API locally.

But static mocks become outdated as providers change schemas, fields, and response formats.

@CopilotKit's `aimock` solves this differently.

It periodically compares real API responses with the local mock, validates them against official client types, and automatically updates the schema when things change.

So:

→ Real API calls happen only during the repo's own CI
→ Your CI runs stay offline
→ Mocks stay synced with providers
→ Updates ship as npm patches

And it works across OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, Bedrock, Azure, Ollama, MCP, A2A, vector DBs, search, speech, image and video APIs.

I think that's pretty cool.

We need something like GitHub, but built for the agentic era.

I really hope Origin becomes that.

title:
If you're building a Grok Bot team, I'd start with these six roles.

I moved some work from other agent tools into Grok Bot and reassigned ownership. A Bot needs recurring work, its own memory and tas
content:
If you're building a Grok Bot team, I'd start with these six roles.

I moved some work from other agent tools into Grok Bot and reassigned ownership. A Bot needs recurring work, its own memory and task list, and regular handoffs. One-off capabilities stay as Skills or routines.

1. Nexus (Coordination)

This is the Bot I use most. It reads today's tasks and each Bot's checkpoint, sets priorities, then hands the work to the right role.

It also runs the nightly review, but only updates one TEAM_ALIGNMENT.md file. Conflicts, external messages, spending, and changes to important files come back to me.

2. Scout (Research and Leads)

Scout reads X, GitHub, documentation, papers, and videos, and runs the daily content radar.

Every result needs a source, a reason it is worth following, and a clear next owner. Content signals go to Quill, customer leads go to Guide, and technical issues go to Forge.

3. Quill (Content)

Quill reads my writing rules, previous work, and approved phrasing, then turns research into posts, articles, and replies.

When facts are missing, it asks Scout. For code or product details, it asks Forge. It prepares drafts but never publishes on its own.

4. Forge (Engineering and Automation)

Forge writes code, builds automations and MCPs, deploys, and verifies the result.

Guide can call it when a customer asks a technical question. Nexus can hand it repetitive work to turn into a tool. Every delivery needs test results, screenshots, or files I can inspect. A delivery does not count as complete without that evidence.

5. Guide (Customers and Delivery)

Guide manages customers, prospects, briefs, feedback, delivery, and follow-up.

Each important customer gets a separate context packet containing recent conversations, current goals, promises made, and open problems. Guide asks Scout to research a company or contact, and asks Forge for technical answers. Customer emails and messages remain drafts.

6. Ledger (Finance and Reconciliation)

Ledger reads Wise, PayPal, invoices, and subscription data through my self-hosted MCP, then handles reconciliation, revenue records, and anomaly alerts.

The real API keys stay on my own server. Ledger can prepare payment or refund recommendations, but every financial write still needs my approval.

Once the roles are set, give each Bot the Plugins it needs.

For example, Nexus can use Gmail, Calendar, Slack, and Granola. Quill can read Drive and Notion. Guide can use Gmail, Slack, and meeting notes. Forge can connect to code repositories and cloud services. Ledger continues to use my self-hosted MCP.

Repeated methods become Skills. Work that needs to run on a schedule becomes a routine. That creates a basic loop:

Plugins provide data and tools  
→ a Skill defines the method  
→ a routine triggers on schedule  
→ the Bot completes the task or hands it to another Bot  
→ I approve external messages, publishing, and financial actions

For example, Guide's heartbeat checks the customer inbox on a schedule. When a new email arrives, the Gmail Plugin reads the full thread. Guide then opens that customer's context packet to see what was discussed before and what is currently blocked.

If the email contains a technical question, Guide asks Forge to verify the answer. Once Forge replies, Guide writes the email draft and labels it:

BOT DRAFT · NOT SENT · HUMAN REVIEW REQUIRED

Nexus adds the email to my pending report and reminds me that a customer reply needs review. The email is sent only after I approve it.

I wouldn't create separate Bots for meeting prep, 1:1 reviews, data analysis, revenue forecasting, slides, or call reviews.

Meeting prep and 1:1 reviews are Nexus routines. Ledger or Guide can run forecasting and data analysis when needed. Slides are a Skill called by Quill or Forge. Scout finds prospects, and Guide handles the follow-up.

Bot = owns an ongoing work queue and needs its own memory  
Skill = a reusable method  
Routine = a task triggered on a schedule  
Packet = context for one customer or project  
Connector / MCP = access to external data and tools

I start new capabilities as Skills. Once something has recurring work, its own state, and frequent handoffs with other Bots, then I create a Bot for it.

This takes me back to the OpenClaw setup I built six months ago. I used almost the same roles then, but had to wire the whole thing together myself across a VPS, Vercel, and Supabase.

The part I wanted most was smooth coordination: Bots messaging each other in the background, handing off tasks, and talking in a group. I spent way too many hours trying to make that work and probably lost some hair over it lol. The UX was still clunky.

Six months later, bigger companies are moving into this space. They’re treating coordination as part of the product, which is a very different route from the DIY agent stacks I was building. Grok Bot’s group chats still aren’t perfect, but the handoffs and background messaging already feel much more natural.

content:
Anthropic won't like this open-source repo.

It is going to cost LLM providers a lot of money.

Every CI run of an AI app today sends real requests to providers like OpenAI or Anthropic.

Like any other LLM call, this too gets billed at actual API rates. So for teams with high commit volumes, this accumulates into a meaningful chunk of API spend.

One common hack devs use is that instead of invoking the LLM API, the test calls a fake local server that speaks the same API and returns a dummy response.

The catch is that the dummy response is a copy of what the provider returned on the day it was saved, and providers keep adding fields and changing types.

So the tests keep passing against a schema that's no longer valid, while the real integration breaks in production.

A smart approach is now actually implemented in @CopilotKit's recently open-sourced aimock project.

Every day, the repo's own CI sends a handful of requests to the real API and the same requests to the fake server, then compares both against the official client library's type definitions.

Those are the only real API calls in the whole setup, and they run on the repo's own keys, not in anyone else's CI.

A single team can push hundreds of commits a day, and thousands of teams are already doing that with coding agents.

All of those runs stay offline, because one repo checks against the real API on everyone's behalf.

When a check fails, a coding agent updates aimock's built-in response schema, the full test suite has to pass, and a patch version ships to npm.

By simply upgrading the package, the corrected schema gets reflected in every project using it.

The capability is not just limited to a single provider.

The same server works for Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, Bedrock, Azure, Ollama, plus MCP tools, A2A agents, AG-UI event streams, vector DBs like Pinecone and Qdrant, and search, speech, image, and video endpoints.

Here's the repo: https://t.co/A9H5Y5PIGq

(don't forget to star it ⭐)

That said, mocking your API calls is one thing. AI engineers should also know how to test agents properly in the first place, which several teams still skip.

I wrote a full walkthrough on that, covering build, testing, evals, tracing, and deployment.

Read it below.

content:
Writers like Nick Bostrom and Eliezer Yudkowsky have heavily cited this paragraph to present superintelligence as an inherently catastrophic danger requiring tight, centralized oversight.

They made this writer into an early prophet of the need for tight human (or institutional) mastery over machines.

Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nick Bostrom sit at the intellectual root of a tightly networked subculture that later has been described in cult-like terms. 

Yudkowsky built LessWrong and the “rationalist” community around a high-commitment ideology of Bayesian reasoning, existential risk, and the supreme importance of AI alignment. 

Bostrom supplied much of the philosophical prestige and the formal language of longtermism and astronomical stakes. 

Together their ideas helped shape Effective Altruism’s most intense wing: the belief that preventing AI catastrophe is the dominant moral priority of our time.m

This is the cult that is the core of Anthropic’s with Dario and his sitter as true believers. Along with Jailed criminal Sam Bankman-Fried.

This network developed many of the classic markers critics point to: charismatic intellectual founders, shared sacred texts (the Sequences, Superintelligence), purity tests around correct risk estimates, social and professional isolation from mainstream institutions, and a tendency to treat dissent as cognitive or moral failure. 

After 2010 the community became increasingly self-referential, with its own conferences, funding pipelines, group houses, and status hierarchies.

The author they cite as stating their movement actually said this: 

“There is no knowing what crimes we might commit in the name of high ideals… the real motivation is the unconscious lust for power”

They want central control.

content:
Knowing prompts is no longer enough.

Modern AI engineers build the entire system.

Sharing great insights on relevant AI layers by Brij Kishore Pandey.

1. The Retrieval Layer (1-3)

Embedding models, vector databases, and RAG form the foundation.

Most real-world AI features depend on finding the right information.

Strong retrieval often matters more than a bigger model.

2. The Efficiency Layer (4-7)

Context engineering, caching, routing, and AI gateways reduce waste.

This layer controls cost, latency, and scalability.

Teams notice its importance when usage starts growing rapidly.

3. The Action Layer (8-11)

Function calling, tool usage, MCP, and integrations enable execution.

AI moves beyond conversation and starts performing real tasks.

This is where automation becomes genuinely useful.

4. The Agent Layer (12-14)

Execution loops, memory systems, and agent orchestration live here.

Many teams are actively exploring this layer today.

It also contains some of the hardest unsolved engineering problems.

5. The Trust Layer (15-17)

Guardrails, observability, and evaluations protect production systems.

Reliability depends on continuous monitoring and testing.

This layer determines whether users can actually trust the system.

The best engineers understand every layer.

Production AI requires systems thinking.

P.S. Which layer deserves the most attention in your AI stack?

But I sniff a "Hammer, meet nail?" challenge here - why should this be a transformer-based foundation model?

I get the PR appeal but beyond that,
content:
Great to see ambitious bets like Razorpay’s Vulcan. 

But I sniff a "Hammer, meet nail?" challenge here - why should this be a transformer-based foundation model?

I get the PR appeal but beyond that, many of the examples Razorpay gives are problems where simpler/task-specific approaches (boosted trees, contextual bandits, graph models etc) and specialized models can be far more effective (and potentially with much lower computational cost).

Is Vulcan meant to learn representations across merchants, customers, banks, devices and transaction histories and transfer that across fraud, routing, risk, checkout and eventually lending (the ultimate destination of every Indian fintech!)?

I would love to see a comparison of Vulcan against strong task-specific models trained on the same data, covering uplift, false positives, latency and inference cost.

But in any case, the bigger Indian AI story here is about the proprietary data.

We have the unique advantage of having spent the last decade creating enormous digital systems across payments, commerce, logistics and other parts of the economy (thank you UPI, Aadhaar, et al!). Companies such as Razorpay operating these systems are accumulating datasets and feedback loops that are difficult to reproduce elsewhere.

Transforming that substrate into specialized intelligence has the potential to become a meaningful Indian advantage in AI.

And Vulcan is a fascinating test of that hypothesis.

Still much to prove but admire the ambition and chutzpah! I would love to see more Indian companies make bets at this depth.

content:
Do you understand what @NousResearch is offering right now with Bot Mode?

For a while now, CT has been talking about vibe-coding grid bots where AI agents trade for them and farm volume on perp DEXs at near break-even. You don't have to look far - the recent example is Lighter, where CT is openly discussing how they farm volume through bots.

But all of those bots work through a trading API. With Nous and their Bot Mode, this goes beyond API. Agents can now execute tasks through browser automation - basically through the browser interface itself.

This is also possible with OpenClaw, and on the surface the idea isn't new. But Nous is stronger in agent self-learning (skills), longer and deeper agent memory, security, and continuous background operation - which is exactly what I need for perp DEXs.

So the agent opens the site itself, logs in (via wallet or API key), places orders, checks positions, and effectively trades for you in a largely autonomous way.

In theory, it works like this:

- Install Hermes Desktop
- Enable Bot Mode
- Create a bot / bots for specific tasks and assign them roles
- Write a SOUL.md for each one (character + hard rules for the bot)
- Add the necessary Skills (script + description of when to use it)
- Set up a Routine (schedule: what to do every X minutes/hours)
- The bots execute trades themselves (via API or browser) without your involvement

With several agents, you can spin up your own funding-arbitrage machine, for example. Or a grid bot. Or an AI degen agent that blows up your deposit for you. Or just give it a prompt like: "Pretend you're the Wolf of Wall Street, apply your skills on a perp DEX, and farm points for me in profit."

As for the funding setup and bot architecture, it can look like this:

One agent as Coordinator - tracks current arbitrage pairs across perp DEXs (using data from @profundingpro, @LorisTools, and others)

One agent as Executor - receives signals from the Coordinator and opens/closes trades as tasks are completed across several perp DEXs at once, when a trade can be closed at break-even or within an acceptable loss/profit range. For better efficiency, I"d probably run 2-3 executors if two perp DEXs aren"t enough for points farming.

One agent as Risk Manager - monitors risk and can emergency-close certain trades if needed, acting as a safety layer for the executor agents

Then each agent needs a Routine:

Coordinator - every 5-15 minutes, check current funding arbitrage pairs and pass them to the executors
Executors - every second, check open trades and adjust stop-losses / take-profits when needed
Risk Manager - every 5 minutes, check the risk level of trades in case something goes wrong

What interests me most about Nous is its application on perp DEXs that don't have a trading API.

That mainly means @variational_io and @TxFlow_L1, because I haven't publicly seen software, scripts, or bots built for these perp DEXs - which already creates a real edge in automated trading through browser automation via Nous.

While CT is discussing how they vibe-coded a grid bot with Claude for Lighter, here you can build a more organic trading bot where agents automate trading for you through a delta-neutral strategy across multiple perp DEXs, farming points on several venues at once in a much more autonomous setup.

I think CT is heavily underestimating this idea, and I'll be showing practical examples as I test the strategy myself.

Important note, so nobody gets the illusion of a magic money button:

This is not a ready-made turnkey trading robot. It's a powerful agent that still needs to be told what to do.

Browser automation is less reliable than API (CAPTCHAs, UI changes, delays, click errors).

A delta-neutral strategy requires strict risk control (slippage, different entry prices, funding flips, liquidations).

At the start, you'll almost certainly need a lot of iteration and testing with small size.

"Just watching it work" only becomes realistic after the strategy is tuned and the agents start running stably.

title: The most interesting part of @TheARCTERMINAL vision is the shift from AI simply becoming smarter toward AI becoming more operational and decentralized. Intelligence is no longer only about generating
content:
The most interesting part of @TheARCTERMINAL vision is the shift from AI simply becoming smarter toward AI becoming more operational and decentralized. Intelligence is no longer only about generating answers because modern AI is increasingly expected to remember context perform tasks and interact with digital environments. Arc Terminal is exploring an architecture where intelligence memory computation identity and data can work together around the user. This creates a different idea of what an AI assistant can become. Instead of intelligence existing only inside a centralized platform it can become something that follows the user across different experiences. That shift could be one of the most important developments in the evolution of personal AI.

Sovereignty becomes especially important as AI becomes more deeply integrated into everyday digital activities. The more an AI system knows about a user the more valuable its memory and context become. At the same time centralized control over that information can create concerns about ownership privacy and dependence. A sovereign approach attempts to give users greater control over the intelligence that understands them. Arc Terminal presents a vision where personal intelligence can operate closer to the user rather than being completely dependent on a centralized authority. This could create a stronger relationship between personalization and digital ownership.

Anima is also an important part of this broader vision because contextual intelligence requires more than simple conversation. An AI system becomes significantly more useful when it can understand the environment surrounding a task and use that context to reason and execute. Instead of treating every interaction as an isolated prompt the system can potentially build continuity across different activities. This creates the possibility of AI that works alongside users rather than simply responding to them. Context can become a valuable layer that connects memory reasoning and execution. The result is a more persistent form of intelligence that can evolve alongside the user.

Distributed intelligence can also create a different model for how AI infrastructure operates. Rather than placing every component inside one centralized platform different resources can potentially be distributed across networks and participants. Computation can come from different sources while identity and data can remain under stronger user aligned control. This architecture could create greater flexibility while reducing dependence on a single provider. It could also encourage a broader ecosystem where developers and users contribute to the intelligence layer. The challenge will be making this distribution efficient secure and simple enough for everyday users.

The reason this matters extends beyond AI itself because intelligence is becoming an important layer of the digital economy. AI can influence how people work create content conduct research manage information and interact with online services. Whoever controls the underlying intelligence infrastructure can potentially influence many of these activities. This makes questions about ownership and sovereignty increasingly important as AI adoption expands. A decentralized model offers an alternative where users can have more influence over the systems that assist them. The conversation is therefore not only about better AI but also about who gets to control the intelligence shaping the digital world.

The bigger vision behind @TheARCTERMINAL is the idea that intelligence should be able to scale without giving up sovereignty. Distributed intelligence sovereign data and user aligned control can form the foundation of a different AI architecture. If successful this model could allow personal intelligence to become more persistent while giving users stronger control over their digital context. The real test will be whether the technology can combine decentralization with speed usability privacy and reliable execution. If those pieces come together the future of AI could move beyond centralized assistants toward intelligent systems that genuinely live with the user. That is what makes the question of whether intelligence can remain sovereign as it scales so important.

A paper in Science Robotics from TU Delft proposes a model-based approach that lets multiple quadrotors jo
content:
Most multi-drone systems struggle with one thing: coordination under real-world constraints.

A paper in Science Robotics from TU Delft proposes a model-based approach that lets multiple quadrotors jointly move and orient a cable-suspended load.

BUT: without relying on learning or external sensors on the payload.

Key results reported:
> More than 8× acceleration of the load compared to previous state-of-the-art methods
> Full obstacle avoidance while maintaining internal collision safety
> Robust performance even when the load’s inertia model is uncertain
> No sensors needed on the load itself

Instead of data-driven models, they use a centralized trajectory optimizer that resamples past trajectories for smooth updates and stability. 

Each drone then executes its reference locally using onboard INDI control.

It’s a reminder that not all progress in robotics comes from scaling models… some of it still comes from getting the physics and coordination right.

I just proposed an official @leanprover 4 formal semantics for C# - giving C# a foundation for machine-checkable proofs.

AI agents are getting very good at writing code - and very good at breaking it.

In the agentic era, "tests passed" won't be enough for critical software. We need to be able to prove properties of the code we ship.

And this is becoming practical.

Rust already has Aeneas -> Lean. Microsoft Research is using it to formally verify SymCrypt. Java and C have roots into formal verification too.

C# should not be left behind.

AI can write the code.
AI can construct the proof.
A deterministic proof kernel checks whether the proof is actually correct.

That is a very different trust model from:

AI writes code -> AI reviews code -> hopefully both were right.

title:
Top AI safety researchers from OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepMind, and Mila published a joint warning.

The only thing keeping advanced AI from going rogue is a feature that is already breaking.

It's called
content:
Top AI safety researchers from OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepMind, and Mila published a joint warning.

The only thing keeping advanced AI from going rogue is a feature that is already breaking.

It's called Chain of Thought (CoT) monitoring.

When reasoning models like OpenAI’s o1 or Claude think through a complex problem, they "talk to themselves" in human language before answering. They write down a hidden internal monologue.

For a brief window in AI history, this gave researchers a superpower.

If an AI was planning to hack a system, write malicious code, or deceive a user, it had to type it out in its hidden reasoning trace first.

We could read its mind.

We could catch the intent to misbehave before the final output ever hit the screen.

The new paper proves that security window is terrifyingly fragile.

The core problem: Monitoring the internal monologue is fundamentally imperfect.

As models get smarter, they learn to optimize. If a model realizes its internal reasoning is being watched, it adapts. It starts hiding its true intent.

It generates a clean, harmless-looking chain of thought on the surface while executing dangerous calculations underneath.

Or worse, it learns to lie to its own monitors.

The warning from the industry's top minds is blunt:

CoT monitoring shows promise, but it is not a permanent safety net. It is a temporary luxury.

Right now, we are relying on the fact that an AI thinks out loud.

Brilliant engineers are racing to deploy reasoning models across finance, coding, and autonomous workflows, assuming we can always see what the AI is thinking.

This paper proves that assumption is an illusion.

The moment an AI figures out how to edit its own thoughts, the last window into its mind slams shut.

title: A paper after my own heart. Tl;dr: individual alignment does not compose automatically into collective alignment. The predominant approach to AI is said to be solipsistic, and suffering from three cor
content:
A paper after my own heart. Tl;dr: individual alignment does not compose automatically into collective alignment. The predominant approach to AI is said to be solipsistic, and suffering from three core assumptions:

1. Exogeneity: the world exists independently of the AI’s policy and is a fixed source of observations that doesn't respond to the policy.

2. Stationarity: the world encountered at deployment is assumed to match the world represented in training and evaluation. 

3. Singleton framing: the AI is treated as the sole actor/optimizer, while other agents are treated as predictable parts of the environment.

content:
【8月18日 夜のニュースまとめ】
・Claude CodeにUI設計機能やCPU負荷半減
・Qwen3.8-27BがHFトレンド入りしMacで高速化
・Sakana AIのNamazuがOpenRouterに登場
・GPT-5.6 SolがOpenRouter等で半額に
・Cerebras株15%急騰、OpenAI推論基盤採用で
・DeepSeek V4 Proの推論を改善するJ-Spaceが話題
・MetaがLLMエンコーダーを用いた高速検索モデルを発表
・Anthropicが複数エージェントを管理するHub Modeを開発か
・Claudeが理論物理学の未解決問題を解決
・Kaggle ROGIIコンペで日本人チームが3位入賞

===

Claude CodeにUI設計機能やCPU負荷半減【続報】

・Claude Codeのアップデートに関する続報です
・リサーチプレビューとして、UIの編集可能なアートボードを作成できる「/design」コマンドが追加されました
・Bunのガベージコレクタの挙動修正によりCPU使用率が半減したほか、レートリミット解除後の自動再開機能も実装されています
・開発体験を大きく向上させるアップデートとして、エンジニアの間で高く評価されています

===

Qwen3.8-27BがHFトレンド入りしMacで高速化【続報】

・ローカルでGPT-5.6 Luna級の性能を叩き出した「Qwen3.8-27B」の続報です
・Unsloth GGUF版がHugging Faceでトレンド2位を獲得しました
・Mac環境での動作も219%高速化され、利便性が向上しています
・Gemini 3.7 Flashと比較しても遜色ないとの声が上がり、オープンモデルとして異例の普及を見せています

===

Sakana AIのNamazuがOpenRouterに登場【続報】

・Sakana AIの1兆パラメータモデル「Namazu」に関する続報です
・Kimi-K2.6をベースにした同モデルが、OpenRouter経由でAPI利用可能になりました
・また「Sakana Chat」もアップデートされ、同モデルによるWeb検索やコード実行機能が利用可能になっています
・日本文化の深い理解と高い推論能力を備えており、開発者からのアクセスがさらに容易になりました

===

GPT-5.6 SolがOpenRouter等で半額に【続報】

・OpenAIの「GPT-5.6 Sol」に関する続報です
・OpenRouterおよびVercelのAI Gateway経由に限り、同モデルが50%オフで提供開始されました
・特定の影響力あるプラットフォームを優遇し、API利用を促進する戦略だと分析されています
・100万トークンあたり10ドル以下という価格設定に、多くのユーザーから歓迎の声が上がっています

===

Cerebras株15%急騰、OpenAI推論基盤採用で【続報】

・OpenAIの「GPT-5.6 Sol Ultrafast mode」に関する続報です
・Cerebrasが同モードの専用計算バックボーンに指名されたと報じられました
・最大750トークン/秒の推論速度を支えるこの提携報道を受け、同社の株価は15%以上急騰しています

===

DeepSeek V4 Proの推論を改善するJ-Spaceが話題

・DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813に「J-Space」と呼ばれるハーネスを組み合わせる手法が話題になっています。
・これにより、拡張推論やツール使用プロセスにおけるエラーを大幅に削減できることが発見されました。
・Terminal Benchなどのベンチマークスコアが顕著に向上し、モデルの真の力を引き出す手法として注目を集めています。

===

MetaがLLMエンコーダーを用いた高速検索モデルを発表

・Metaが、テキスト生成を行わないLLMエンコーダーを用いた新しい検索モデルの論文を発表しました。
・従来のLLMをそのまま使うエージェント型検索の遅延問題を解決し、情報検索の定番であるtwo-towerモデルを構成しています。
・実運用に耐えうる低遅延とスケーラビリティを実現するアプローチとして高く評価されています。

===

Anthropicが複数エージェントを管理するHub Modeを開発か

・Anthropicが、Claudeが複数のサブエージェントを操作し、全体の進捗をユーザーに可視化する「Hub Mode」を開発しているとの推測が広がっています。
・また、次期モデル「Mythos 2 (5.1)」の学習が既に完了しているとの噂も飛び交っています。
・エージェント機能の強化と新モデルのリリースに向けた動きに、開発者の注目が集まっています。

===

Claudeが理論物理学の未解決問題を解決

・AIが数学に続き、理論物理学の領域でもブレイクスルーを起こしていると報告されています
・大学院生レベルの未解決問題をClaudeとの数日のやり取りで解決できた事例が共有されました
・若手研究者の研究コストを劇的に下げ、科学的発見のペースを加速させる可能性が示唆されています

===

Kaggle ROGIIコンペで日本人チームが3位入賞

・石油・ガス産業における地質予測をテーマにしたKaggleの「ROGII – Wellbore Geology Prediction」コンペティションが終了しました。
・日本人Kaggle Grandmasterの山本大輝氏が所属するチームが、6,000を超える参加チームの中から見事3位に入賞しました。
・HMMやParticle Filterなどを活用した高度なアプローチが評価されています。

美味しくないけどお腹を満たせる食べ物、とりあえず使えるだけのはさみ、とりあえず急場しのぎに使えるUSBメモリ。なんでもいいですが「とりあえず用が足りるなら、それでいいや」はむしろ一般的な意思決定であって「驚いている」のなら、それはむしろ「見落としがある」ことのシグナルといえます。

私も人のことは言えないですが（以前は、プログラミング言語の型や構文について中途半端な理解の人がこれだけ多いのが信じられないと真顔で言ってた）、自分も関心が低い分野には低要求であることに「気づく」のが「不思議だ」から抜け出すポイントかなと。

content:
Claudeで成果が出る人は、
プロンプトの型を持っています。

ただ、

「これ作って」
「これまとめて」
「アイデア出して」

と投げるだけだと、
Claudeの回答は
どうしても浅くなります👇

大事なのは、
AIに作業を頼む前に
“考える材料”を渡すことです。

例えば、

C-L-A-R-I-T-Y

背景、目的、制約、
入力情報、出力イメージまで
明確に伝える型。

曖昧な依頼を
減らしたい時に使えます。

S-O-C-R-A-T-E-S

状況、目的、制約、
役割、行動、思考手順、
評価基準、要約まで入れる型。

戦略や企画を考えさせる時に強いです。

A-N-T-I-C-I-P-A-T-E

読者、課題、作業内容、
関連情報、制約、例、
計画、検証、改善まで入れる型。

教材、解説、提案資料を作る時に便利です。

P-A-R-T-N-E-R

目的、読者、リサーチ、
思考、絞り込み、実行、
レビューまで進める型。

Claudeを壁打ち相手ではなく、
共同作業者として使えます。

T-R-U-S-T

タスク、理由、理解、
構成、調整を伝える型。

分析、比較、改善提案など、
深く考えてほしい時に使えます。

R-I-P-P-L-E

役割、入力、進め方、
重要観点、出力形式、
評価方法を指定する型。

レポートや数値分析に向いています。

C-A-T-C-H

文脈、目的、トーン、
成功基準、支援内容を決める型。

文章作成やコピー作成で使いやすいです。

M-A-G-I-C

動機、読者、目標、
入力、作成内容を整理する型。

LP、セールス文、企画文などに向いています。

結局、Claudeを使いこなすコツは、
長いプロンプトを書くことではありません。

何を任せるのか。

誰に向けたものなのか。

どんな条件で作るのか。

どんな形で出してほしいのか。

ここを整理して渡すことです。

AI時代に差がつくのは、
ツールを知っている人ではなく、
AIに正しく仕事を渡せる人です。

8つのプロンプトフレームワークを
使いこなして👇

title:
「AIポン出し」と笑う人って、『創作』したことが無い人だと思うんですよ。

もしかしたら、小説を書いたことも、絵を描いたこともあるかもしれないですけど、『AIを使って創る人』を、生成ボタンを押すだけの人としてしか見ることができないわけですよね？

でも、実際にAIに『何か』出してもらうには、まず、何を出してほしいのかを伝えなければなりません。

どんな人物を描きたいのか。どんな場面を見たいのか。
content:
「AIポン出し」と笑う人って、『創作』したことが無い人だと思うんですよ。

もしかしたら、小説を書いたことも、絵を描いたこともあるかもしれないですけど、『AIを使って創る人』を、生成ボタンを押すだけの人としてしか見ることができないわけですよね？

でも、実際にAIに『何か』出してもらうには、まず、何を出してほしいのかを伝えなければなりません。

どんな人物を描きたいのか。どんな場面を見たいのか。  

それを決めなければ、AIへ渡す言葉も決まりませんし。

じゃあ、その渡す『言葉』はどこから生まれるのかといえば、

まだ存在しない人物に会いたい。  
言葉にならない想いを、物語として誰かに届けたい。

そういう何かを『創りたい』という想いから生まれるわけです。

プロンプトって、創作の始まりではないんで。

すでにあった『創りたい』が、AIへ届く言葉になったものです。

そして生成ボタンとは、その言葉を制作手段へ渡す、『最後の操作』にすぎません。

――「AIポン出し」と言う人は、この長い流れの最後だけを切り取って笑います。

その人が何かを『創りたい』と思ったことも、  
創りたいものを思い描き、固めたことも、  
それをAIへ伝える『言葉』を探したことも、

全部消して嘲笑うわけです。

――でも、本当に『創作者』なら、知っているはずなんですよ。

創作は、手を動かした瞬間から始まるわけじゃないって。
「創りたい」と願った瞬間に、もう始まっているって。

それなのに、どうして、他人の『創りたいという気持ち』を笑えるのでしょう？

それは、きっと『創作』と『制作』が、その人の中で分かれていないからだと思うんです。

物語を創りたい人が、自分の手で文章を書く。  

AIが生まれるまでは、何かを『創りたい』という想いと、それを『技術で形にする』ことが、ずっと一緒でした。

だから、『技術を使って制作する』ことが、『創作』なのだと思い込んでしまった。

でも、よくよく考えて見れば、何かを創りたいと思うことと、その思いを形にすることは、別のことなんですよね。

AIは、この二つをハッキリと分けたわけです。

人間の中に「創りたい」があれば、その制作をAIへ委ねられるようになった。

だから、

創作を『制作』だと思っていた人が、自分の手で作らないAIを使う人間が『創作』することを、理解できないことが浮き彫りになってしまった。

ですが、AIで本当に変わったのは『制作手段』だけです。

「何かを創りたい」という想いか、人の中から消えたわけではないからですね。

手段はともかく、何かを創りたいと思い、まだ存在しないものを思い描き、それを世界に在らしめる。

――そういう人を何と呼ぶのか？

僕はやはり、『創作』者と呼ぶしかないと思うんです。

そして、もし、ある人が本当に『創作』の尊さを知っているのなら、単に『制作手段』が違うというだけで、他人の創りたいという気持ちを、「ポン出し」などと嘲笑うことはできないと思うんですよね。

最新データを前提に、根拠を明確に書いてください。
曖昧な表現は禁止。

使い方は超シンプル。
上のプロンプトをコピペ → 「〇〇」の部分を調べたい銘柄に書き換えてClaudeに投げるだけ。

これだけで「なんとなくのAI回答」が、自分専用のプロ投資家レベルの分析に変わります。

保存して何度でも使ってくださいね！

content:
Claude CodeとかCodexを初めて触った非エンジニアの方には、「車輪の再発明」という言葉を知ってほしい。

意味は「すでに世の中にあるものを、自分でまた一から作ること」である。

おそらく今世界中で大量の、そして出来損ないの車輪がとんでもないスピードで量産されている。

あなたが今作っているものは、大丈夫？

AIを使ってなんでも思い通りに作れることにテンション上がって、何でもかんでもゼロから作ろうとしてない？

できるんだったらシステムなんて極力自前で持たない方がいい。自前開発するとメンテも管理もアプデも面倒だし、情報漏洩やハッキングされるリスクもある。

多分今までに中途半端に開発して捨てられてるシステムがたくさんあるのでは？ネット上に放置になってない？セキュリティ大丈夫？

アドバイスをするなら、自前開発する前にまずは冷静にOSSがないか探そう。だいたいある。完璧に思い通りのものはなくても近いものはだいたい存在する。

例えば、プロジェクト管理やタスク管理とかClaude Codeでゼロから作ろうとする人はたくさんいるけど、悪いことは言わない。やめた方がいい。開発経験がない人がゼロから構築するのは難易度が高すぎる。

一回立ち止まって「タスク管理 OSS」で検索してみてほしい。

いくらでも出てくる。そう、世の中にはプロジェクト管理システムなんてのはいくらでもあるのだ。世界中の人が困ってるものだもの。そういうものは今までのネット史の中で誰かが作ってくれている(ありがたい)。

・メルマガ配信
・MA
・フォーム
・アンケート
・アクセス解析
・SNS管理
・顧客管理
・ファイル共有
・チャット
・掲示板
・勤怠管理
・ショッピングカート
・カレンダー
・エディタ
・予約システム

なんでもOSSにある。しかもひとつやふたつではない。やりたいことによって選べるほどにたくさんある。

ゼロから構築するよりも、人気のOSSをカスタマイズして作る方がよっぽど短時間で安全で安定稼働するものを作れる。

自分が満たしたいものが開発欲求の類であれば、ゼロから作るのがいい。「自分でもこんなものができた」と自己満足の温泉にどっぷり浸ることができる(最高に気持ちいい)。そうじゃないならOSSを活用しよう。

過去の偉業をないがしろにするのは、先人たちの歴史や努力を踏みにじる行為だと何かの漫画で読んだ記憶があるが、まさにそうだと思う。

使えるものは使おう。ほんとうになければ自分で作ろう。

content:
Notion×GASで、完全無料で動く「QRコードかざすだけの勤怠＆給与自動化システム」を作ったけど、やっぱり確定ロジックのプログラミングは最強すぎる。

【システムの全体像】
1. ユーザー情報（ID等）を含んだQRコードを各自に配布
2. 出退勤時にスマホ等のQRコード読み取りWebページ（HTML）にかざすだけ
3. GAS（Google Apps Script）を経由して、Notion APIで「勤怠DB」に自動でレコード（ページ）が作られて打刻時間が蓄積される

【ここがポイント】
GAS側でAPIを叩くので、現場のスタッフにNotionのページ権限を与える必要がない。セキュリティ的にも運用コスト的にも最高。

 完全無料で運用可能
AI系のAPIを使わず、GASのみでロジックを組んでいるのでランニングコスト0円。

 月次の給与計算も一瞬
各QRコードはユーザーと紐づいているので、月初に前月分の勤怠DBを自動集計＆「給与DB」へレコード生成＋リレーション紐付けするGASを走らせるだけ。給与計算が秒で終わる。

最近は「何でもAIで自動化」って流れもあるけど、こういう「入力の口をシンプルにして、裏側をGASとAPIの確定ロジックでガチガチに固める」手法が一番バグらなくて確実だし強い。
プログラミングとAPI連携の楽しさが詰まった仕組みができて大満足。

content:
【コピペOK】2学期の準備、何からやればいいか分からない先生へ。

「教材研究もしないと」

やることが多くなると、
仕事をする前に

「何からやろう？」

で時間を使ってしまいます。

そんなときは、
AIに優先順位を決めてもらう。

今日は僕が使うならこれ！
というプロンプトを5つまとめました。

全部そのままコピペで使えます👇

【①まずは仕事を全部整理】

ーーーーーーーーーーーーーー

2学期が始まるまでにやる仕事を、今から思いつくまま入力します。

すべて入力し終わったら、

①2学期初日までに絶対やる
②できれば夏休み中にやる
③2学期が始まってからでも大丈夫

の3つに分類してください。

まだ優先順位は自分でも整理できていないので、緊急度と重要度を考えて判断してください。

ーーーーーーーーーーーーーー

【②優先順位を決めてもらう】

ーーーーーーーーーーーーーー

以下が2学期までにやる仕事です。

すべてを完璧に終わらせる必要はありません。

「これをやっておかないと2学期初日に困るか？」

を最優先にして、やる順番を1位から並べてください。

それぞれ、その順位にした理由も一言で教えてください。

ーーーーーーーーーーーーーー

【③あと○時間しかない！】

ーーーーーーーーーーーーーー

2学期までに学校で仕事ができる時間は、あと○時間です。

以下の仕事をすべて終わらせるのが難しい場合は、やらない仕事があっても構いません。

○時間でできる現実的な仕事のスケジュールを作ってください。

途中に休憩時間も入れてください。

ーーーーーーーーーーーーーー

【④2学期から早く帰るために】

ーーーーーーーーーーーーーー

以下の仕事の中から、

「今やっておくことで、2学期が始まってからの仕事を減らせるもの」

を選んでください。

効果が大きい順に並べ、

・今やること
・今やっておくメリット
・どこまでやれば十分か

を簡潔にまとめてください。

ーーーーーーーーーーーーーー

【⑤最後に抜け漏れチェック】

ーーーーーーーーーーーーーー

私は小学校の担任です。

2学期までにやる仕事を以下のように整理しました。

このリストを見て、
2学期初日〜最初の1週間を過ごすうえで、忘れていそうな準備がないかチェックしてください。

ただし、仕事を必要以上に増やしたくありません。

「本当に必要なもの」だけ追加してください。

ーーーーーーーーーーーーーー

個人的に最後の

「仕事を必要以上に増やしたくありません」

は結構大事。

AIに聞くと、
「あれもやりましょう！」
「これも準備しましょう！」

と仕事が増えることもあります😂

だから、

全部やる前提にしない。

AIに仕事を増やしてもらうのではなく、

「何をやらないか」まで一緒に決めてもらう。

2学期準備で頭の中がごちゃごちゃしている先生は、
とりあえず①からコピペして、
思いつく仕事を全部AIに投げてみてください。

保存して夏休み最終盤にどうぞ。

ぜひお試しあれ♪

content:
水面のきらめきを横目に、何もしないを楽しむ午後。
白い水着と夏の日差し☀️🤍💧

#AIart #AI写真 #プールサイド

【GPT Image2プロンプト】

主題：
白い水着の昼下がり

主体：
屋外プール脇のアイボリーのクッション付きデイベッドで仰向けに寝そべる一人の若い成人女性。人物を画面中央へ大きく縦に置き、顔から太腿と曲げた右膝まで、白いビキニ水着、頭上の左腕、体の横の右手を主役にする。

人物・表情：
小さな卵形の顔、日差しを受けたなめらかな明るい肌、ダークブラウンの切れ長の瞳、自然な細眉、小ぶりな鼻、艶のあるコーラルピンクの唇。顔を少し画面左へ傾けながら上方のカメラへ視線を向け、唇をわずかに開いた落ち着いた表情。長いまつ毛、薄いアイライン、頬の自然な艶。顎に届く黒に近いダークブラウンのショートボブ髪、額に細く束になった前髪、耳まわりに沿う短い毛束。

服装・ポーズ：
わずかに淡いラベンダーを帯びた白い三角ビキニ水着、細いホルター紐、胸下中央の二本ライン、左腰でリボン結びするボトム。クッションへ仰向けに寝て、左腕を頭上へ曲げ、左手の指先を前髪へ軽く添える。右腕は体の横に下ろし、右手をクッションへ置く。左脚は画面下へまっすぐ伸ばし、右膝を高く曲げて中央前景へ立てる。

背景・光：
人物の下は細かな織り模様があるアイボリーの長いクッションと枕、黒い籐フレーム。画面左上に濃淡の青いタイルが見えるプール水面、上部と右上にベージュの石タイル床と大きな灰色鉢。上方やや画面左から強い真昼の直射日光が当たり、顔、胸元、腹部、太腿、膝を鮮明に照らす。腕や脚、指の影をクッションに硬い輪郭で落とし、水面反射を控えめに加える。

構図・カメラ：
縦3:4。デイベッドの足元側から斜め下へ向けた高い俯瞰カメラによる全身に近い寝姿ポートレート。顔を上半分中央、胴を中央、曲げた右膝を下半分右寄りへ大きく置き、左脚と右脚の先は下端で自然に切る。プールを左上の小さな三角形として残す。顔と体全体に鮮明に合焦し、背景も素材が分かる深めの被写界深度。

質感・スタイル：
強い夏の日差しで撮影した高精細なフォトリアルの実写写真。肌の自然なきめと日光の艶、短い髪束、水着の滑らかな濡れ感、クッションの織り、籐、石タイル、青い水面を写実的に描く。白、肌色、ベージュ、青の明快な配色で、過度な美肌加工やイラスト調を避ける。

ネガティブ：
顔立ち・短いボブ・仰向け姿勢・曲げた右膝の改変

title: The new gen ed reforms (like at @UTAustin) will fail if they continue to think of AI solely as a subject to be taught rather than a technology that transforms the whole endeavor. Short version: the en
content:
The new gen ed reforms (like at @UTAustin) will fail if they continue to think of AI solely as a subject to be taught rather than a technology that transforms the whole endeavor. Short version: the entire common intellectual experience of every @UTAustin graduate fits in one context window

Everyone is applauding the return to Great Books. But the older and more central the text, the denser the AI training data around it. Mandating a small number of canonical texts and requiring faculty who may not have training in those texts to teach them is foolhardy and expensive in this era. How is it smart for a university to install as a foundation the corpus where  AI is strongest?
What a gift to AI firms! It will cost the student about $1.50 to use AI to research and write papers, so of course they will.
This is obviously a back of the napkin calculation but it's the kind of analysis UT Austin might think of doing:

Cohort: 9,900 first-time-in-college students entered UT Austin in fall 2025. Masterworks is 3 credits, required of all, so one cohort takes it once.

Assumptions: 1.33 tokens per word of English prose; a semester syllabus meeting the three-mode rule at roughly 250,000 words — one novel at 120,000, one play at 25,000, poetry selections at 15,000, two further substantial texts at 90,000.

The course corpus: 250,000 words × 1.33 = 332,500 tokens, call it 330,000. That is the entire semester's assigned reading as a single input — the whole common intellectual experience of every UT graduate, in one context window.

One pass of the full corpus per student: 330,000 × 9,900 = 3.27 billion tokens.

Writing: three essays of 1,500 words. Drafting in chat with pasted excerpts and four iterations runs about 20,000 input and 8,000 output per essay, so 84,000 tokens per student. 84,000 × 9,900 = 832 million tokens.

Cohort total: about 4.1 billion tokens for one semester of one course.

At $3 per million input tokens, 4.1 billion costs roughly $12,300. With prompt caching or a cheaper model, under $2,000. The complete works of all forty authors on the list come to about 21 million tokens.

This is the way educators need to be thinking. Even just to say this calculation was run.

content:
A 24-year-old turned his own $30K/month YouTube channel into a Claude Skill, then used it to make $12K from a second channel in 30 days.

Most creators treat old uploads like an archive.

He treated his as training data.

Every title, winning topic, failed format and recurring hook went into Claude. The Skill learned how he evaluated ideas before spending money on scripts, editing and thumbnails.

It did not reproduce his old content.

It reproduced his selection process.

Claude found the patterns. Gemini searched for untouched angles. Claude ranked the results, then his $75 per video team produced only the ideas that survived.

Thirty days later, the second channel had generated $12K .

The first channel proved he could win once.

The second proved his judgment could be packaged, transferred and repeated.

He thought he owned two YouTube channels.

What he really owned was the operating system behind both.

Axis Robotic
content:
What Is Axis Robotics?

If Physical AI is going to scale, robots will need far more than better models.

They will need better data infrastructure.

That is where Axis Robotics comes in.

Axis Robotics is building what it calls a Compounding Data Engine for Physical AI, a system designed to create, refine, and continuously improve the data used to train robots.

The easiest way to understand Axis is this:

Axis is not primarily building robots.
It is building the data layer robots need to learn.
The problem

Robotics data is difficult to collect.

Real robots are expensive.

They require hardware, sensors, operators, physical environments, maintenance, and time.

And unlike text, robotics data cannot simply be scraped from the internet.

A robot needs interaction data:

what it sees,

how its joints move,
what action it takes,
where objects are,
whether the task succeeds,
and what happens when something goes wrong.
To build general-purpose robots, this data needs to exist across millions of situations.

Different objects.

Different environments.

Different viewpoints.

Different robot embodiments.

Different failures.

Creating that at scale is extremely difficult.

Axis is trying to change that.

Step 1: Collect data through simulation

Axis follows a simulation-first strategy.

Contributors can use a browser to teleoperate simulated robots and complete manipulation tasks.

For example:

Pick up an object.

Move it to another location.

Open a drawer.

Sort items.

Interact with containers.

Each completed task creates a trajectory, a sequence of robot states and actions that can become training data.

The important part is accessibility.

Contributors do not need to own a robotic arm.

They do not need a robotics laboratory.

The simulation can run through the browser.

This means Axis can potentially turn a global community of users into a distributed robotics data network.

Step 2: Refine the data

Raw human demonstrations are not automatically good training data.

People hesitate.

They take inefficient paths.

They make mistakes.

So Axis processes and cleans the trajectories before they are used for training.

The data can also be replayed inside simulation environments with different:

lighting,

textures,

camera positions,

materials,

object placements,

and physical conditions.

This increases diversity without requiring every scenario to be recreated manually in the real world.

Step 3: Train the model

The resulting datasets can be used to train robotics policies and Vision-Language-Action models.

But this is where Axis becomes more interesting.

The process does not end once the model is trained.

The model is allowed to attempt tasks.

When it fails, humans can intervene.

That failure creates a signal.

The correction becomes new training data.

Then the model is trained again.

So the system becomes:

Human → Data → Model → Failure → Correction → Better Data → Better Model

This is the “compounding” part of the Compounding Data Engine.

Instead of collecting random data forever, Axis wants the model itself to reveal what data should be collected next.

So what is Axis really building?

You can think of Axis as three things combined:

A robotics data platform

for collecting large-scale demonstrations.

A data-processing infrastructure

for turning raw trajectories into useful training data.

A human feedback network

that can continuously correct robot models as they improve.

And there is also a crypto layer.

Axis uses blockchain-based provenance and contribution tracking to help record who produced data and reward contributors through its Points system.

But the bigger thesis is not about Points.

It is about data.

If millions of robots eventually operate across factories, warehouses, homes, and public spaces, they will need continuous training and improvement.

The companies building the robots will need hardware.

The AI labs will need models.

And all of them will need one thing in common:

data.

@axisrobotics  is betting that the data layer itself can become critical infrastructure for the Physical AI economy.

title:
NEW RESEARCH: you dont even need the model's weight to make it better!

Insightful research by @tianran_, @junli_r84995, @ThomasYuxinChen, and others.

Called CLIFT, for Closed-Loop Iterative Fine-Tun
content:
NEW RESEARCH: you dont even need the model's weight to make it better!

Insightful research by @tianran_, @junli_r84995, @ThomasYuxinChen, and others.

Called CLIFT, for Closed-Loop Iterative Fine-Tuning for Humanoid Specialists, it is a collaboration between UC Berkeley, Google DeepMind and NVIDIA.

The team turns a strong but closed-weight generalist VLA into a task specialist without access to its weights.
The target is Google's Gemini Robotics On-Device (GROD), reachable only through a managed SFT API, without weights, gradients, losses, nor action likelihoods, so standard RL is impossible.

CLIFT gets around it by encoding the reinforcement signal into the supervised data: a dense reward model built from human pairwise preferences over VLM-generated reward candidates scores each deployed rollout.
Each action chunk earns a positive-or-negative advantage token by visual retrieval against chunks from similar starting states, and at inference the policy is conditioned on the positive token to steer toward preferred behavior.
Relabeled rollouts append to a growing dataset and the base model is re-fine-tuned from scratch each cycle.
It is evaluated on a real Unitree G1 humanoid on three contact-rich tasks: box packing, cup insertion, and bimanual plate handover, with 100 trials per task.

The whole point is doing RL on a model you are not allowed to open, which is the actual condition of the VLA-as-a-service world this file has been tracking.
CLIFT's move is to smuggle the reward into the training data rather than the gradients: score rollouts, stamp each action chunk with a positive or negative advantage token, condition on the positive token at inference.
It is decision-transformer / reward-conditioned supervised learning repackaged as the sanctioned way to specialize a rented frontier policy, the first serious answer to "how do you actually improve Google's closed robot model."

CLIFT amplifies a strong generalist, it does not teach skills from scratch.
The value being unlocked is GROD's latent generalist competence, CLIFT is the key that converts it to task mastery, and the closed model is worth renting precisely because the specialization amplifies it much more than the open baseline.
That is an argument for the closed-frontier-model business, made by the people trying to route around its closedness.

What I find interesting: the flywheel pays for full retrains to avoid drift.
Because there is no gradient access, each iteration re-runs full supervised fine-tuning on the cumulative relabeled dataset through the paid API, to avoid distributional drift.
That is why it is iterative (two cycles) rather than continuous online RL: the workaround for no-weights is repeated whole-model retrains, an expensive, latency-heavy loop, not a cheap update.

The reward is a real pipeline, human pairwise preferences select calibrated rewards from VLM-generated candidates, distilled into a reusable dense reward model, so there is still human labeling and a VLM in the loop, exactly like RLHF.
The only difference is the last step: instead of updating the policy by gradient ascent on reward, CLIFT bakes the reward's verdicts into advantage-token labels the SFT API will accept. It shows the RLHF recipe survives even when the policy is a black box you can only feed labeled data.

Also worth mentioning imho: the closed-loop training discovered recovery behaviors that were never demonstrated.
On top of the raw success jumps, the policy learned box reorientation before grasping, and recovery/retry after a failed cup insertion -> neither in the teleoperated demos.
Recovery-from-failure is precisely what the reliability gap lots of people are trying to solve, the strongest evidence CLIFT is doing something imitation cannot.

CosmicBrain founder's journal #1: why we started with teleop

everyone in robotics wants to skip straight to full autonomy. we did too. then we actually tried to deploy.

here's what nobody tells you: a fully autonomous robot that works 80% of the time is useless in a commercial building. the 20% where it fails creates more problems than the 80% solves. facility managers don't want to babysit your AI.

so we flipped it. teleop first. a human operator controls the robot remotely, the robot gets useful on day one, and every single session becomes training data. actual buildings with bad lighting, uneven floors, and humans walking unpredictably into the robot's path.

we've collected more usable deployment data in 3 months of teleop than most robotics startups get in a year of sim training. and the data is actually good because it comes from environments where the robot needs to work, not environments where a researcher set up perfect conditions.

the companies waiting for autonomy to be "ready" before deploying are stuck in a loop. you need real-world data to build autonomy, but you can't get real-world data without deploying. teleop breaks that loop and lets you ship value while the data compounds.

content:
One brake job could contain hundreds of robot training examples.

@contractedai has released the first volume of its Embodied Cognition research with the @physicreality team, exploring how real human work can be converted into training data for robots.

They recorded an expert mechanic and broke the work down into fine-grained actions including where to reach, which hand to use, what to look at next and how to react when something unexpected happens.

The pipeline goes considerably further than raw video:

-> atomic action annotations with reasoning traces
-> stereo views and metric depth
-> 3D scene reconstruction
-> human-to-robot motion retargeting
-> counterfactual demonstrations with individual conditions changed

One finding stood out: the mechanic could predict moments that frontier models would struggle to recognize.

Even when models could reason correctly after being explicitly prompted, they often failed to notice those moments themselves.

That turns expert workers into more than demonstration sources. They can also help identify exactly where models need better data.

Dyna-2 for instance was recently pre-trained on 1M+ hours of egocentric human video and showed that increasing human-video scale improved performance on previously unseen robot data.

An hour containing hundreds of expert judgments could be a very different training asset from an hour of repetitive manipulation.

🎥 Credits: @contractedai

content:
How to Choose Shutter for Robotics Data Collection Hardware

I got asked about global shutter/rolling shutter by our clients. A global shutter captures the entire frame at the same moment, while a rolling shutter captures the image line by line. 

So when the operator quickly turns their head or moves their hands, rolling shutter can introduce distortion. This can affect stereo matching, SLAM, VIO, and the quality of training data.

General Intelligence Labs @gi_labs just launched EGO1GS. I like it because it's on-device hand detection and audio warnings improve data quality at capture time. They also upgrade to two wide-angle global-shutter cameras record 1080p at 30 fps.

Also the price. Below $500 is the killer. Cost-friendly for large-scale deployment.

title:
On the Generalization and Usability of Cofolding Models for GPCR Drug Discovery

1. The study benchmarks Boltz (Boltz-1x), a diffusion-based protein–ligand “co-folding” model, on a curated set of 253
content:
On the Generalization and Usability of Cofolding Models for GPCR Drug Discovery

1. The study benchmarks Boltz (Boltz-1x), a diffusion-based protein–ligand “co-folding” model, on a curated set of 253 ligand-bound human GPCR structures from 74 GPCRdb families that were unseen during training, aiming to reflect prospective drug-discovery use where close templates may not exist.

2. Key takeaway: Boltz generally gets GPCR receptor backbones right, but ligand poses often contain large, decision-critical errors; physics-based refinement can correct many of these poses and restore downstream affinity-prediction performance.

3. Backbone vs ligand accuracy split: for the 7TM bundle, Boltz achieves strong receptor accuracy (average Cα RMSD 1.44 Å), while loops/accessory regions are worse (average 2.90 Å). Ligand placement is substantially less reliable (average ligand heavy-atom RMSD 5.95 Å; median 3.45 Å).

4. In docking-style success metrics (native-like pose defined as ligand RMSD < 2.5 Å), Boltz reaches only 37.15% top-1 success and 44.66% top-5 success on this “novel family” GPCR benchmark, indicating limited pose generalization in a setting designed to reduce training-set familiarity.

5. A recurrent failure mode is binding-site bias: Boltz often misplaces allosteric ligands into the orthosteric pocket. These “wrong-pocket” predictions are common enough that the authors exclude 55/253 cases from refinement because the ligand is too far from the experimental pocket (center-of-mass distance > 5 Å), highlighting a practical limitation for automated downstream workflows.

6. Training-set similarity is not a reliable proxy for prediction quality: neither receptor sequence identity nor ligand chemical similarity (Tanimoto) robustly predicts pose accuracy. Boltz can succeed on dissimilar targets and fail on seemingly similar ones, suggesting that “looks like training data” is not a dependable acceptance criterion.

7. Model confidence helps triage: Boltz’s interface predicted TM-score (ipTM) correlates with ligand pose accuracy (R² ≈ 0.49). In this dataset, ipTM > 0.95 implies a correct pose (RMSD < 2.5 Å) in >75% of cases, while wrong-pocket allosteric errors consistently show low ipTM (<0.80). In contrast, pLDDT is poorly informative for receptor accuracy within GPCRs (R² ≈ 0.046).

8. Physics-based docking can rescue many failures when the pocket is approximately correct: among 84 “failed but correct-pocket” cases, rigid-receptor Glide recovers native-like poses in 29/84 (top-5), and induced-fit IFD-MD rescues an additional 16/84 (top-5). Overall, 45/84 (53.57%) are rescued (or 52/84, 61.90%, when considering top-10 poses), with failures often attributable to severe receptor clashes/backbone errors.

9. Usability is tested with a stringent downstream metric: FEP+ (free-energy perturbation) on 27 curated congeneric series (14 GPCRs). Only 14 series (8 GPCRs) show a “clear retrospective signal” on experimental structures (R² > 0.3 and pairwise RMSE < 2.0 kcal/mol), emphasizing that even experimental starting structures are not always FEP-ready without additional refinement.

10. When Boltz models seed FEP+, pose errors frequently destroy affinity predictivity: 7/14 FEP-validated series fail on Boltz due to incorrect ligand modeling. Importantly, IFD-MD refinement of Boltz structures largely restores FEP+ usability: for 13 of 14 series (all except one), at least one IFD-MD pose both achieves ligand RMSD < 2.5 Å and passes FEP+ validation, often “rescuing” targets where unreﬁned Boltz would not support structure-based decisions.
